62. In the case of an election petition, based on allegation of commission of corrupt or illegal practice or illegal acts such as capturing of booths, rigging and strapping of votes, the burden of proof is on the election petitioner and that burden does never shift. A charge of corrupt and illegal practice are regarded as quasi-criminal in character and the standard of proof required for establishment of corrupt practice is the same as is required to establish a criminal offence. Strict proof is demanded from the person bringing the charge to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. 

 63. The allegation of corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act requires strict proof as because the consequence are not only very serious but also penal in nature. On proof of any corrupt practice it is not only the election of the returned candidate which is declared to be void and set aside but the candidate himself or his agent or any other person, if found to have committed the offence of the commission of corrupt practice, may be punished with imprisonment. It is for this reason strict proof of such allegation of corrupt practice is insisted and not mere preponderance of probabilities as in civil action. Suspicion, however strong, cannot take the plea of proof. 

 66. Through the testimonies of PW. 1, the election petitioner (unsuccessful candidate), P.W. 2.the Polling Agent of Domarchar Polling Station, P.W. 4, Polling Agent of Shambupura Polling Station and P.W.6, the Polling Agent of Satgram Government Polling Station, a faint attempt was made for proof of commission of corrupt practices such as capturing of polling booths by the supporters of the returned candidate but the testimonies of the PWs were totally demolished by the testimonies of the RWs who through their convincing, reliable and satisfactory testimonies could successfully prove that the polling was peaceful RW. 1 the returned candidate, RW. 2. the principal election agent of returned candidate, RW 3, a voter. RW 4.Chairman of Union Parishad for two terms.RW 5.RW 6.RW 7.RW 8, RW 9 all voters. RW 10 an ex-member of the Parliament from Bangladesh Nationalist Party. RW 12. polling agent of the returned candidate, RW 13, a voter and Union Parishad Member, RW 14. the Headmaster of a High School and Presiding Officer of Domarchar polling station, RW 15. Professor of Government Sadat Ali College and Presiding Officer Shambupura polling station. RW 18, Magistrate, RW 19, Professor of Government Sadat Ali College and Presiding Officer Satgram Government Primary School polling station testified that polling in Shambupura polling station, Domarchar polling station and Satgram polling station had been although peaceful and no untoward incident took place. The testimonies are consistent and inspire confidence. 

 "Before dealing with these contentions, we may recall, what this court has repeatedly said, that an order for inspection and recount of the ballot papers cannot be made as a matter of course. The reason is twofold. Firstly such an order affects the secrecy of the ballot which under the law is not to be lightly disturbed. Secondly, the Rules provide an elaborate procedure contains so many statutory checks and effective safeguards against trickery, mistakes and fraud in counting, that it can be called almost foolproof. Although no hard and fast rule can be laid down, yet the broad guidelines, as discernible from the decisions of this court, may be indicated thus: 

 89. On 12.06.1996 polls in Shambupura polling station and Domarchar polling station were held and the election was held peacefully. Election of the above stated two polling stations was not adjourned as adjourned including Satgram polling station. No allegation, no complaint was ever made to Presiding Officer, Assistant Returning Officer, Superintendment of Police, the Magistrate and also to Chief Election Commissioner as to the Commission of any corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act allegedly committed by the returned candidate, his agent or any other per-son or his supporters. No complaint, no allegation was ever laid with respect to rigging, capturing of booths and strapping of votes, proper and illegal acceptance of invalid ballot papers as valid ballot papers in favour of the returned candidate by the Presiding Officer and the other officers who were on election duty. There is no contemporaneous papers, documents and materials manifesting that on the conclusion of poll at Shambupura polling station and Domarchar polling stations on 12.06.1996, the unsuccessful candidate made any prayer even an approach to the Presiding Officer and the Returning Officer to recount ballot papers which were very much permitted under Article 36(5)(b) and 37(5)(a) of the Order. The election petitioner (unsuccessful candidate) on the conclusion of the poll held at 6 adjourned polling stations on 19.06.1996 by laying an application before the Returning Officer brought allegations against the successful candidate and his supporters in commission of illegal acts and corrupt practice only in respect of Satgram polling station and in the application also no allegations had been launched with respect to any illegal acts or corrupt practices allegedly committed by the returned candidate and improper acceptance of invalid votes as valid votes in favour of the returned candidate by the Presiding Officer and other election officials at Shambupura and Domarchar polling stations. In the event of any commission of illegal acts or corrupt practices by the returned candidate his agents, and supporters and improper and illegal counting of invalid votes as valid votes in favour of the returned candidate by the Presiding Officer and other election officials, then the unsuccessful candidate would have definitely brought allegations to the election officials and other authorities. Non launching of allegations with respect to commission of illegal acts, corrupt practices and improper reception of invalid votes as valid votes in favour of the returned candidate. The unsuccessful candidate in the election petition, for the first time, brought vague allegations of the alleged commission of illegal acts and corrupt or illegal practices and improper counting of invalid votes as valid votes by the Presiding Officer in favour of the returned candidate without supplying full particulars and reliable data's. It is well settled that full particulars must be supplied and in support of those particulars there must be strict proof by which the Tribunal would come to a decision whether the foundation had been at all laid for recounting of ballot papers on reopening ballot boxes. Care must be taken to see that the election petitioner (unsuccessful candidate) do not get a chance to make a roving or fishing inquiry into the ballot boxes. 

 91. Before taking the course of recounting ballot papers on reopening ballot boxes the Election Tribunal must be prima facie satisfied on the basis of the statements made in the election petition and the legal evidence adduced and other materials on record that the scrutiny and the recounting of ballot papers has become a material issue and is imperatively necessary to resolve the controversy and to do complete and effectual justice between the parties. An Election Tribunal can be satisfied not on the basis of mere allegation unsupported by substantial evidence but only on the basis of proof to the hilt beyond all reasonable doubt. The Tribunal if so satisfied, is required to record reasons as to how it came to be satisfied. Every judicial decision must he based on reasons and the reasons must be disclosed in the judgment itself. From the order No. 77 dated 9.12.1998 calling the ballot papers and other election materials and the judgment itself it appears that the Election Tribunal made no attempt at all to give finding whether he was prima facie satisfied regarding the credibility of the evidence adduced before it and other materials on record that recounting became imperative to decide the controversy. Mere decision that to secure ends of justice recounting of ballot papers are necessary will not do. The learned Tribunal without recording any reason simply stated that for ends of justice, recounting was necessary. A Judge can be satisfied on the basis of proof and not on the basis of mere vague allegation. There is absolutely no proof in this case to support the allegations on the basis of which the scrutiny and recounting of ballot papers can be made.
